title: Block close: the sea
hookLine: the Talmud is called a sea: no one crosses it, everyone can swim

lines: YOU DON'T HAVE TO CROSS IT.
cards: Some books get called a library. Some get called a mountain. The Talmud, in Jewish speech, is sometimes called a sea: yam haTalmud, the sea of Talmud.
It's a picture of size and of depth, and of something else too. Nobody crosses a sea in an afternoon. Nobody drinks it dry.
But you don't have to cross it to be in it. You only have to walk in from the beach.

teach.b: Look back along the shore we've walked. A written Torah, and an oral teaching beside it, written down when it might have been lost.
The tannaim, who gave the Mishnah its words, and the amoraim, who discussed them line by line. The orders: seeds, appointed times, women, damages, holy things, purities.
Then how the page works: a case and its voices, a sugya, a question left to stand, Rashi in the inner margin and Tosafot in the outer, the minority view kept for a later day.
Then how law is decided: halakha, the way you walk, through the codes to questions about electricity and saving life.

And these last days, living with it: a finished tractate, an open page, the ways of peace, hard passages, jokes, flawed heroes, a lost partner, a wounded sage, a teacher who left, and a pomegranate. Now the sea.
No one crosses it. Even a siyum, the party for a finished tractate, ends with words that promise a return: hadran alakh, we will come back to you. Finishing isn't leaving.
Everyone can swim. One mishnah, one line, one partner, and you're in the water; nobody checks your credentials at the beach.

Its currents are arguments that haven't stopped: Hillel and Shammai, a voice from heaven turned away, a question about a bird with one foot on each side of a line. You don't stand outside a sea and admire it. You get wet.

how: Jews learn Talmud in many ways: a daily page, a weekly class, a partner, a teacher, a single mishnah. At a siyum, learners often recite hadran, a promise to return to what they finished.

practice: Bring to mind one thing from this block that stayed with you: a word, a story, a person. Let it float there, and turn it over once: what does it ask of you? One wave is enough; you don't have to hold the whole sea.
